ubo_and_aml_profiling.statutory_law_governance: Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009 (AML/CFT Act 2009, Public Act 2009 No. 35), as amended by the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Amendment Acts 2017 and 2023, particularly Part 2 (customer due diligence and AML/CFT programmes), sections 20 to 22A (political exposure, enhanced CDD, and PEP obligations) and Schedule 2 (reporting entities encompassing financial institutions); Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism (Definitions) Regulations 2011 (beneficial ownership deemed to arise at a threshold of 25% or more of the controlling interests); Financial Service Providers (Registration and Dispute Resolution) Act 2008 (FSPA 2008, Public Act 2008 No. 97) governing registration of providers of financial services including receivable factoring; Companies Act 1993 (Public Act 1993 No. 105), sections 22 to 27 (name reservation and review) and sections 87 to 92 (share and beneficial ownership records); Companies Regulations 1994; Sanctions Act 2019 (Public Act 2019 No. 3); Russia Sanctions Act 2022; Terrorism Suppression Act 2002; and the Financial Markets Authority (FMA) and Department of Internal Affairs (DIA) AML/CFT supervision codes, together with FATF Recommendations 24 and 25 on transparency and beneficial ownership of legal persons (New Zealand is a full FATF member).
ubo_and_aml_profiling.ubo_disclosure_level: Government_Only_Access - Beneficial ownership information and internal UBO matrices are obtained through mandatory AML/CFT customer due diligence and disclosed to the Companies Office and AML/CFT supervisors (FMA, DIA, Reserve Bank of New Zealand) and law-enforcement agencies upon lawful request; the public Companies Register displays only director identities, service addresses and company particulars, not individual shareholder or UBO names.

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Hague Apostille OR Consular Legalization of the notarial certificate

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Hague Apostille on the notarial certificate OR Consular Legalization

ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory enhanced due diligence on Politically Exposed Persons under section 20 of the AML/CFT Act 2009, covering foreign PEPs (F-PEPs), domestic PEPs (D-PEPs) and international-organization PEPs (IO-PEPs), with prescribed 90-day verification refreshment for higher-risk relationships; mandatory negative screening against the New Zealand Sanctions Register maintained under the Sanctions Act 2019 and the Russia Sanctions Act 2022, the United Nations Security Council Consolidated List, the United Kingdom and European Union consolidated sanctions lists as a cross-reference benchmark, and the United States Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List as an international market-practice requirement; adverse-media monitoring; FATF High-Risk Jurisdictions Subject to a Call for Action integrated into customer-risk rating; and mandatory suspicious transaction reporting (STR) to the New Zealand Financial Intelligence Unit (NZFIU) hosted by the New Zealand Police.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: New Zealand Companies Office - Name Reservation portal and Companies Register (https://www.companiesoffice.govt.nz / https://app.companiesoffice.govt.nz); cross-verification against the Financial Service Providers Register (FSP Register) at https://www.fsp-register.companiesoffice.govt.nz
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Official statutory languages are English and te reo Maori; a proposed company name must be capable of being entered in Latin script and must not be identical or confusingly similar to an existing registered name or reserved name under sections 20-22 of the Companies Act 1993; company names may be registered in English or Maori, but non-Latin characters must be transliterated/romanized into the English alphabet; the corporate suffix 'Limited', 'Ltd', or a statutory-approved equivalent is mandatory; adjectival and structural rules prohibit names that imply incorporation without limitation, government patronage, or a regulated activity absent applicable consent.
prohibited_and_sensitive_tokens: Factoring (where implying a licensed financial-services undertaking without FSP registration)
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: A name reservation holds the name for 20 working days from approval; if the company is not incorporated within that period the reservation lapses automatically and the name reverts to the open pool, requiring a fresh reservation application (no statutory extension is available). Upon refusal, the applicant may lodge a written request for review with the Registrar of Companies within 20 working days of the refusal under section 27 of the Companies Act 1993; the Registrar is obliged to reconsider the application, and if the name is again refused the applicant may appeal to the High Court of New Zealand. Parallel lodging of an alternative proposed name during the review period is permitted; for financial-service names, the Registrar will defer to the Financial Markets Authority on consent-sensitive tokens.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: Conditionally permissible with significant constraints: section 186 of the Companies Act 1993 requires every company to maintain a registered office in New Zealand at a physical street address where documents may be served during ordinary business hours; a pure mail-forwarding 'virtual office' without a physical reception and service-of-process acceptance does not satisfy this obligation and is unacceptable to the Financial Markets Authority for an FSP-registered factoring business. A serviced physical office (Auckland, Wellington, or Christchurch) with dedicated meeting facilities, physical records retention, and a registered agent accepting service is recommended; a virtual-only presence is treated as a serious substance deficiency that may disqualify the company from FSP registration and materially undermine the 'tax-exempt zone' structuring.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: 60-75% probability of an unannounced on-site compliance inspection by the Financial Markets Authority (FMA) or Department of Internal Affairs within the first 18 months of operation, escalating to a near-certain (90%) inspection within 24 months where nominee shareholders, a 'tax-exempt zone' characterization, or non-resident UBOs are present; expected frequency is 1-2 physical inspections per 24-month cycle, with enhanced likelihood for ISIC 6492 trade-finance activities due to the medium-risk enhanced AML/CFT tier.

incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: Companies Act 1993 (New Zealand), ss 15 (capacity), 16 (constitution), 19 (registration requirements), 20 (application for registration), 21 (Commission to register), 23 (registered office requirements), 28 (charter and constitution optional), 122 (appointment of directors), 126 (director duties), 161 (financial reporting obligations); Financial Service Providers (Registration and Disputes Resolution) Act 2008 if providing financial services; Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009 for obliged entities; Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance Act 2003 if extending consumer credit (not applicable to pure trade factoring between businesses unless ancillary).
incorporation_legal_framework.competent_registry_authority: New Zealand Companies Office, Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE), Auckland/Christchurch/Wellington, administered via the New Zealand Companies Register electronic online portal (www.companiesoffice.govt.nz).
incorporation_legal_framework.statutory_filing_instrument: Form R/A — Application for Registration of a Company (Incorporation Application) under Section 20 of the Companies Act 1993; accompanied by a New Zealand Companies Office consent to act as director and shareholder consent forms, and a registered office address consent.
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: For an International Company (tax-exempt zone, non-resident owned) incorporated under the standard New Zealand Companies Act regime: no minimum paid-up capital is prescribed by statute; capital may be zero or nominal. No escrow account is required at incorporation. If the company will hold an FMA financial services licence or rely on factoring-related licensing exemptions, the Registrar may require evidence of solvency or a minimum net tangible equity, typically NZD 50,000 (approx. USD 30,500) for financial services licence applicants; funds must be held in a New Zealand bank account or as otherwise directed by the Financial Markets Authority. For ordinary factoring/credit under trade receivables, no statutory paid-up capital escrow applies.
incorporation_legal_framework.pro_forma_first_board_resolution_en: FIRST RESOLUTION OF THE BOARD OF DIRECTORS OF [COMPANY NAME], an International Company registered under the Companies Act 1993 of New Zealand. RESOLVED: (1) That the company shall adopt the articles of association filed with the New Zealand Companies Office and shall comply with the Companies Act 1993. (2) That the subscription for the shares issued on incorporation is approved, and the allotment of shares to the subscriber/member as recorded in the register of members is ratified. (3) That the registered office of the company within New Zealand be and is hereby fixed as [Address, City, New Zealand], and the Registrar of Companies is authorised to record the same. (4) That the directors appointed named in the application for registration, namely [NAME] and [NAME], are ratified and continue as directors; any additional directors appointed by the subscriber be and are hereby elected. (5) That [NAME] be and is hereby appointed as Chairperson, [NAME] as Chief Executive Officer, [NAME] as Chief Financial Officer, and [NAME] as Company Secretary (where required); each shall hold office subject to the Companies Act 1993 and the company's constitution. (6) That the directors are authorised to open bank and escrow accounts with [BANK NAME] in New Zealand and internationally for trade-factoring settlement, with signatories as determined. (7) That the directors are authorised to obtain all required licences including, if applicable, registration under the Financial Service Providers Register, and to engage legal counsel for AML/CFT compliance. (8) That the directors are authorised to execute all filings and agreements for the company's cross-border trade supply chain factoring operations.

step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: New Zealand Companies Office online Name Reservation Portal (www.companiesoffice.govt.nz)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Submit an online name reservation application for the proposed company name (e.g. '[Name] International Finance Limited'). Verify that the name is not identical or confusingly similar to an existing New Zealand name or reserved overseas trademark; the name must not include restricted words such as 'Trust', 'Bank', 'Finance', 'Factoring' or 'Insurance' without consent from the respective regulator. If the proposed name implies regulated financial business, obtain written consent from the Financial Markets Authority and the Reserve Bank of New Zealand before reservation. The reservation is valid for 20 working days. File online, receive a name reservation confirmation, and retain the reference number for the incorporation application.
required_dossiers: Proposed company name (up to 3 alternatives optional)
Name search result document
Consent from Financial Markets Authority if using restricted financial terms
Director's identification: passport or national ID (certified)
Proof of residential address (utility bill or bank statement, issued within last 3 months, certified)
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the name is refused or reserved against, file a further name application with a new distinctive name; request the Registrar to review the refusal under Section 23(3) of the Companies Act 1993; or apply to the Registrar for a formal direction as to allowable words. If refusal is founded on confusing similarity, a written consent from the prior name-holder may be lodged.

step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Legal Practitioner (New Zealand) / New Zealand Companies Office
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Engage a New Zealand-qualified law firm or chartered accountant to draft the constitution (if adopted), the shareholder consents, director consents, and registered office address consent. The constitution may provide for entrenchment provisions, share transfer restrictions, and class rights; otherwise the Companies Act 1993 default rules apply. For an International Company in the tax-exempt zone, include clauses ensuring that control and management remain outside New Zealand for income tax purposes, and that all factoring contracts are denominated and performed offshore or through permitted cross-border arrangements. Draft the Form R/A and electronic filing details; obtain wet-ink or digital signatures from all subscribers and directors. Each director must sign a consent to act as director on the approved official form, which is filed electronically with the Companies Office.
required_dossiers: Constitution (optional but recommended for International Company status)
Form R/A signed
Consent to act as director (Form A4 or online declaration) for each director
Certified passport copies of all subscribers and directors
Registered office consent from the New Zealand registered office provider
Proof of lawful use of business name (if required)
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the Registrar requires corrections under Section 19A (Registrar's power to require information), the solicitor must supply the amended forms within 20 working days; if a director is disqualified under the Companies Act 1993, replace the director and file a new consent; if constitution is defective, amend and re-file before incorporation.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Submission of Incorporation Application to Companies Register
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: New Zealand Companies Office (electronic lodgement via the Companies Register online) — MBIE
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Submit the complete application electronically via the Companies Office web portal by registered users. Pay the filing fee by credit card or direct debit. The system instantly validates the data; the completed incorporation occurs upon certificate issue, normally immediately or within 1-2 working days. The company shall be allocated a New Zealand Business Number (NZBN) and New Zealand Companies Number. Upon registration, the Companies Office automatically uploads the company constitution (if filed) and records directors and shareholders. No notarization is required for local filings, but certified translations into English for foreign passports are required if not in English. For apostille or authentication of foreign documents, use the New Zealand Department of Internal Affairs Authentication Unit after incorporation if required by foreign banks.
required_dossiers: Form R/A Application for Registration complete
Name reservation reference number
Constitution (if adopted)
Consents to act as directors signed by all proposed directors
Shareholder and director identification documents in English or certified translations
Registered office address and consent from the registered office provider
Payment of filing fee (NZD 200 online / approx. USD 134)
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If lodgement is queried, respond through the Companies Office case management portal within the stated deadline (typically 10 working days). If the application is rejected, correct the defective item and resubmit without penalty; if the Registrar requests further information under s 385, provide certified copies within 20 working days. If the certificate is withheld due to AML/CFT doubts, supplement with additional evidence of lawful activity and beneficial ownership.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Issuance of Register of Shareholders, Register of Directors, and Post-Registration Corporate Records
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: New Zealand Companies Office / Directors of the Company in consultation with registered office provider
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: After the certificate of incorporation is issued, the company must prepare and maintain statutory registers: (a) register of shareholders under s 84; (b) register of directors under s 88; (c) register of charges under s 102; and (d) minutes of shareholder and director meetings. Issue share certificates for each subscriber to reflect the allotted shares. Maintain the registers at the registered office or a physical location in New Zealand; if kept elsewhere, a notice must be filed with the Registrar. Obtain an IRD number with Inland Revenue for tax purposes, and register for Goods and Services Tax if annual turnover exceeds NZD 60,000. If the company will be non-resident and tax-exempt, file an IR742 or company tax return confirming non-residency status to maintain the tax-exempt treatment.
required_dossiers: Certificate of Incorporation (issued by Companies Office)
Register of Shareholders (shareholder consents, share allotment ledger)
Register of Directors (with identity documents)
Register of Ultimate Beneficial Owners (as required under the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009 for financial services providers)
Share certificates signed by at least two directors or in accordance with the constitution
IRD registration application (IRD 1 form)
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the Companies Office detects late filing or incorrect register maintenance, rectify the register and file a 'Change of Particulars' form (Form R/S) with supporting declaration; penalties under s 364 can be avoided by voluntary correction before enforcement notice. If foreign ownership/beneficial ownership information is queried by a bank or regulator, provide a certified breakdown of the corporate chain and UBO register extract.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: AML/CFT Programme Adoption and Company Secretary/Compliance Officer Appointment
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Department of Internal Affairs (DIA) / Financial Markets Authority (FMA) — Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Because the company's trade factoring scope is in the medium-risk enhanced AML category, adopt a written AML/CFT compliance programme before commencing operations. This programme must include: (a) risk assessment of customers and products; (b) customer due diligence standards; (c) ongoing due diligence and transaction monitoring procedures; (d) suspicious transaction reporting to the Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU); (e) record-keeping for at least 5 years; and (f) appointment of an AML/CFT Compliance Officer. Register the company on the Financial Service Providers Register (FSPR) under the Financial Service Providers (Registration and Disputes Resolution) Act 2008 if the factoring activities constitute a financial service under Schedule 2 (which includes factoring where credit is provided by way of debt factoring or a similar transaction). If the company is a non-resident provider, exemptions may apply; obtain legal advice and where necessary apply under section 14 of the Financial Service Providers (Registration and Disputes Resolution) Act 2008 for a cessation or exemption. File an annual FSP return and join an approved disputes resolution scheme (e.g. Financial Dispute Resolution Scheme) if registration is required.
required_dossiers: AML/CFT written compliance programme approved by the board
AML/CFT risk assessment matrix
Customer Due Diligence policy and Know-Your-Customer forms
Appointment letter for AML/CFT Compliance Officer
Financial Service Providers Registration application (FSP1), if applicable
Certificate of Incorporation and constitution
Details of directors, shareholders, and ultimate beneficial owners
Registered office address and service address for FSP purposes
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the FSPR refuses registration, revise the business model to exclude New Zealand-resident customers or request a determination under s 15 of the Financial Service Providers (Registration and Disputes Resolution) Act 2008; if the DIA/FMA issues a corrective warning, amend the AML/CFT programme within the timeline set out in the warning notice; contact the Financial Intelligence Unit before filing cross-border wire transfer reports.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Post-Incorporation Filings with Inland Revenue and Optional Escrow/Operating Bank Accounts Opening
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Inland Revenue New Zealand and New Zealand Banks (under Financial Markets Authority and Reserve Bank supervision)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Apply to Inland Revenue for an IRD number (for the entity and, where relevant, for GST and employer obligations). Complete the IRD entity registration online using the NZBN. Provide the Companies Office certificate and board resolution to open a New Zealand bank settlement/escrow account; banks require director ID, beneficial ownership declaration, board resolution, and business plan describing the factoring operations. For cross-border trade receivable factoring, use a segregated client/escrow account to separate funds held for clients from operating funds, in line with the Companies Act 1993 requirements for trust accounts and to mitigate money-laundering risk. If the company is non-resident and claims tax exemption, file an annual income tax return as required to maintain the 'tax-exempt zone' treatment; in New Zealand, an International Company means a non-resident foreign-owned company with a certificate from the Inland Revenue confirming its operations/source are outside New Zealand. Also register for GST if making taxable supplies in New Zealand over NZD 60,000 per annum and if not required, elect to register only if the factoring agreements are to be made with New Zealand counterparties.
required_dossiers: NZBN and Certificate of Incorporation
Board resolution authorising bank account and escrow arrangements
Certified passports of directors, shareholders and UBO declarations
Brief business plan / description of factoring operations (including source of funds)
AML/CFT compliance programme summary
IRD registration confirmation
Registered office address and physical presence details if required by the bank
Statutory registers extract
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the bank account application is deferred or declined due to enhanced due diligence, submit additional evidence of underlying trade invoices, beneficial ownership charts, and proof that the funds originate from lawful international trade; consider establishing client money account through a licensed trustee/registered bank; if Inland Revenue queries residence, file a statement of non-resident status (IR290) and provide evidence that control and management are outside New Zealand.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.competent_industrial_authority: No industrial manufacturing authority is applicable for accounts receivable factoring. For any ancillary physical office/back-office in New Zealand, the local territorial authority (City or District Council) is the consent authority for land use; for any digital/administrative activity, no industrial license is required. For financial services licensing if covered, the Financial Markets Authority and the Companies Office (Financial Service Providers Register) under the Financial Service Providers (Registration and Disputes Resolution) Act 2008. If the company engages in consumer credit or finance company conduct, the Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance Act 2003 and the Reserve Bank of New Zealand's 'responsible lending' code may apply. For cross-border trade factoring, no industrial/services operating physical permit is mandated; still, if the company uses commercial premises, the local council must issue a certificate of occupancy.
industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.operating_license_title: Financial Service Provider (FSP) Registration No. [...] (if factoring is captured as a financial service under Schedule 2 of the Financial Service Providers (Registration and Disputes Resolution) Act 2008), and any required Certificate of Compliance for Money Service/Factoring operations; if using an NZ-registered base, a Business Operations Certificate from the territorial authority is required only if physical premises are used. If factoring is treated as debt collection/credit servicing under the Credit Contracts and Consumer Finance Act 2003, a license under that Act may be relevant but is typically not required for pure business-to-business reverse factoring.

environmental_impact_assessment_eia.agency_name: Environmental Protection Authority of New Zealand (EPA) / local Regional Council for land-use resource consents (under the Resource Management Act 1991).
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.classification_tier: Category Registration / Not required (waived) for office-based factoring and trade finance activities; no statutory EIA required as the operation involves no industrial discharge, no vegetation clearance, no earthworks, and no contaminated site use. If physical premises are leased, a simple resource consent for office use may be required by the local District or City Council; if no new building works, an exemption applies.
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.discharge_and_emissions_standards: Not applicable for factoring activities because the company does not operate a discharge point to air, land, or water. If the company later operates ancillary document-shredding or chip-card production, comply with NES for air quality (NES-AQ), Hazardous Substances (Minimum Degrees of Hazardousness) Regulations 2001, and wastewater standards per regional plan (e.g. suspended solids < 50 mg/L, pH 6-9, oil and grease < 10 mg/L before discharge to municipal sewer); office wastes must be segregated per the Waste Minimisation Act 2008.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.civil_defense_and_occupational_clearance: Fire Safety and Building Compliance: If the company occupies an office, a Building Warrant of Fitness (BWOF) issued under the Building Act 2004 must be maintained by the building owner and displayed; the company must conduct a fire evacuation scheme approved by Fire and Emergency New Zealand (FENZ) if the premises are a workplace with more than 10 employees or high-risk. Occupational Health and Safety: Under the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015, the company must (a) appoint a competent health and safety officer, (b) issue a written health and safety policy, (c) perform hazard identification and risk assessments, (d) provide first-aid kits and trained first-aiders based on headcount, and (e) obtain a WorkplaceSafe New Zealand clearance / worker engagement and participation training if operating from registered commercial premises. Structural load inspections are not required for office use without heavy machinery. Civil defence: prepare a business continuity / civil defense plan (earthquake/storm) and maintain worker protection supplies as recommended by the National Emergency Management Agency. For a tax-exempt offshore managed company, if no physical New Zealand employees exist, no local occupational clearance is needed; still obtain an offshore business address and registered agent certificate.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Inland Revenue Department (IRD) / Te Tari Taake — New Zealand's national tax administration; taxpayer self-service portal: myIR (https://www.ird.govt.nz/myir).
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: A foreign (non-resident) entity must obtain a New Zealand IRD number by filing Form IR742 (Non-Resident Company IRD Number Application) with Inland Revenue, accompanied by certified copy of the certificate of incorporation, registered office details, and director/shareholder particulars. For a Cook Islands International Company (CK_IC), the entity is typically non-resident for New Zealand income tax and requires an IRD number only if it derives New Zealand-source income, carries on business in New Zealand through a fixed establishment or permanent establishment, or registers for GST. The application may be filed by a New Zealand tax agent via myIR; Inland Revenue issues the 8-9 digit IRD number within 5-10 working days following verification. Where New Zealand-source withholding income is anticipated, the company should simultaneously register for non-resident withholding tax (NRWT) obligations.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.default_entity_tax_classification: Tax_Exempt_Zone — a Cook Islands International Company is an offshore entity holding statutorily exempt status under the Cook Islands International Companies Act 1981-82; for New Zealand domestic tax purposes it is treated as a non-resident foreign company subject to entity-level taxation only on New Zealand-source income, with no New Zealand CFC or attribution exposure while outside the controlled-foreign-company perimeter unless controlled by New Zealand residents.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: New Zealand does not operate U.S.-style check-the-box elections. Available statutory mechanisms include: (i) GST grouping election under the Goods and Services Tax Act 1985 s. 55 to treat associated companies as a single GST group; (ii) loss grouping election under Subpart IC of the Income Tax Act 2007 permitting offset of tax losses between commonly owned companies; (iii) hybrid mismatch adjustment elections under Part FM aligned with OECD hybrid rules to neutralize deductible/non-inclusion mismatches; (iv) NRWT tax treaty election to reduce domestic withholding rates; and (v) for non-resident companies, an election to be treated as carrying on business through a New Zealand branch where applicable.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: Goods and Services Tax (GST) — a VAT-style consumption tax under the Goods and Services Tax Act 1985
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: NZD 60,000 of taxable supplies in any 12-month period. Factoring, invoice discounting, and other receivables-financing intermediation services are exempt financial services under the First Schedule of the GST Act 1985, thereby excluded from the taxable-supply threshold calculation. A non-resident cross-border factoring platform supplying services to New Zealand GST-registered businesses with no New Zealand fixed establishment generally has no New Zealand GST registration obligation; registration may be required only for remote services supplied to New Zealand resident consumers (B2C) under the remote-services rules.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: New Zealand imposes no mandatory real-time fiscal clearance, no digital stamping, and no tax-authority API e-invoicing clearance. Electronic invoicing is voluntary and follows the Peppol PINT interoperability framework (e-Invoicing). GST returns and payments are filed electronically via myIR; transactional data is reported on a summary basis rather than transaction-by-transaction. For exported goods, the mandatory digital filing is the Customs Export Declaration lodged through the New Zealand Customs Service Trade Single Window (CUS/BAC electronic declaration).

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: For goods: zero-rated when exported from New Zealand under s. 11(1)(a) of the GST Act 1985, provided the supplier obtains and retains credible evidence of export (customs export declaration, bill of lading or airway bill, insurance and freight documentation) within 28 days of supply and the goods leave New Zealand within 12 months. For services: zero-rated under s. 11A where supplied to a non-resident who is outside New Zealand at the time the services are performed and the services do not relate to New Zealand land or moveable goods situated in New Zealand. Factoring: invoice financing and factoring are exempt financial services rather than zero-rated supplies; consequently the supply is GST-free without input-credit entitlement. Cross-border factoring of receivables originated from non-resident sellers with no New Zealand nexus falls outside the New Zealand GST net entirely and requires no zero-rating claim.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Customs Export Declaration (Electronic CUS/BAC lodged via Trade Single Window)
Bill of Lading or Airway Bill evidencing physical departure of goods from New Zealand
Inward Remittance Certificate or bank SWIFT/MT103 evidence proving receipt of export consideration
Duly executed factoring agreement and assignment of receivables (for cross-border trade receivables)
Commercial invoice and packing list evidencing the underlying exported goods
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: Inland Revenue may reassess GST zero-rating positions within 4 years for a tax return with acceptable disclosure and within 8 years where the return was not provided, was materially incomplete, or involved fraudulent or evasive conduct (Tax Administration Act 1994 s. 108). Unsupported zero-rating attracts reinstatement of the 15% GST plus use-of-money interest, a shortfall penalty of 20% for lack of reasonable care, 40% for gross carelessness, escalating to 100-150% for evasion (ss. 141A-141D TAA 1994), and for invoicing or refund fraud, a criminal fine of up to NZD 250,000 for a company and/or imprisonment of up to 5 years. Exporters are also subject to clawback of input credits previously claimed on exported goods or services if export evidence is later discredited or the goods are re-imported or diverted to domestic consumption.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: New Zealand's Foreign Exchange Control regime is fully liberalised; there are no exchange controls applicable to current account transactions, capital account transactions, profit remittances, or dividend distributions by non-resident-owned entities. The New Zealand Dollar (NZD) is freely convertible onshore and offshore, and non-resident investors may repatriate capital, dividends, interest, and factoring proceeds without prior exchange control approval. Practical hurdles are limited to bank-level anti-money laundering (AML) / know-your-customer (KYC) documentation for the beneficial owner of the International Company, tax residency/withholding obligations for outbound interest and dividends, and the residual requirement to ensure any suspense or settlement accounts are not used to circumvent sanctions screening or anti-money laundering filters.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: There is no statutory requirement in New Zealand for export proceeds to be surrendered to the RBNZ or converted into NZD. Exporters and factoring entities may retain foreign currency proceeds in external accounts indefinitely, and there is no mandatory conversion ratio or repatriation deadline. For trade-supply-chain factoring structures, the only applicable compliance touchpoints are New Zealand's anti-money laundering reporting obligations under the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism (AML/CFT) Act 2009, which require reporting of suspicious transactions and prescribed transactions of NZD 10,000 or more, rather than any FX surrender mandate.

tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.account_class: Cross-Border Settlement and FX Hedging Account

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Feasibility rating: Medium-High for the International Company (CK_IC) conducting cross-border trade receivables factoring, subject to strict structural constraints. New Zealand does not issue FinTech electronic money institution (EMI) licences equivalent to the EU EMI passport; non-bank payment providers must register as 'financial service providers' under the Financial Service Providers (Registration and Dispute Resolution) Act 2008 and, if they hold or control customer funds, be licensed under the Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013 or operate through a registered bank. Offshore digital EMIs (e.g. UK or Lithuanian EMIs) may be viable as ancillary collection/settlement rails, but they cannot provide a New Zealand bank-issued escrow account, cannot execute SWIFT MT103 with a New Zealand BIC in a fully NZD-clearing manner without an underlying NZ correspondent bank, and may trigger regulated credit-activity implications because factoring and reverse factoring constitute a financial service that requires registration and an approved dispute resolution scheme under the Financial Service Providers Act. The recommended approach is to use the Offshore EMI solely for non-NZD collection in jurisdictions where the obligor is resident, while maintaining a core NZD operational account with a Tier 1 New Zealand registered bank.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: New Zealand banks generally do not require directors to appear physically for account opening on a standalone corporate structure. Remote opening is permitted under the AML/CFT Act 2009 and the RBNZ/Financial Markets Authority guidelines provided that the bank can conduct electronic verification of identity and beneficial ownership using reliable, independent sources. However, in practice, Tier 1 New Zealand banks apply internal policy overlays requiring (a) a physical presence of either the director or a New Zealand-based professional introducer (lawyer/accountant) for initial identification, or (b) a live international video interview with a compliance officer, plus certified passport and proof of residential address. Due to the cross-border factoring scope and International Company structure, a physically attending director in Auckland or Wellington is strongly recommended to de-risk the onboarding; if the director cannot travel, appointing a reputable New Zealand corporate services provider or law firm as a 'know-your-customer introducer' with a power of attorney to liaise with the bank materially improves onboarding viability.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: International Company (CK_IC) incorporated in an offshore/low-tax jurisdiction with no physical substance in New Zealand
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: New Zealand Companies Office registration extract; certificate of incorporation; constitution and director register; disclosure of ultimate beneficial owner (UBO) chain to natural persons; substance dossier demonstrating real economic activities in trade-finance operations (employment contracts, office lease, board meeting minutes, trades/ledger data); tax profile and non-tax-resident position; explanation of commercial rationale for the offshore structure.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Factoring and reverse-factoring activities involving cross-border receivables from related or unrelated trade counterparties in multiple jurisdictions
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Complete portfolio register of factored invoices with debtor master files and jurisdiction breakdown; underlying trade contracts, bills of lading/AWBs, proof of delivery and invoices; assignment notices to obligors (or global assignment notice if receivables are on a revolving facility); audited or management accounts showing receivables purchase pricing (discount rates, fees, reserves); a detailed AML/CFT risk assessment of debtor jurisdictions, including sanctions/PEP screening reports for counterparties.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: High turnover through transaction-based payments received into or paid from the corporate operating account, triggering large-value transaction monitoring thresholds (NZD 10,000 and NZD 15,000 under prescribed transaction reporting)
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Transaction monitoring policies approved by the board, including Tier 1 'beneficial owner' disclosure; documented source of funds and source of wealth for each material capital inflow from the settlor or lender; forward trade pipeline and underlying client agreements demonstrating a legitimate trade-finance cycle; reconciliation reporting to the bank for every debit/credit batch; independent AML/CFT audit report (where applicable) and annual declarations supplied to the AML/CFT supervisor.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Escrow Account and trust-related flows from a foreign trust or foundation in the Cook Islands/offshore lineage, raising source-of-funds or tax-evasion concerns
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Trust instrument or foundation deed; evidential chain from trust assets/settlor to incorporation capital and operational funding; external legal opinion confirming that the structure is not a tax evasion or laundering vehicle and that beneficial owners are natural persons of good repute; ongoing periodic UBO attestation; anti-bribery and anti-corruption compliance manual; letters of reference from counterpart banks in the originating jurisdiction.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Potential applicability of the New Zealand Financial Service Providers (Registration and Dispute Resolution) Act 2008 for providing factoring as a financial service
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Evidence of registration on the New Zealand Financial Service Providers Register (FSPR) with the New Zealand Companies Office; membership in an approved dispute resolution scheme (e.g. Financial Dispute Resolution Service); documented compliance programme under the Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013 relevant to debt securities or credit servicing (where applicable); independent counsel opinion delineating that the International Company does not hold an insurance or bank license requirement under section 45 of the Insurance (Prudential Supervision) Act 2010 and is not a deposit-taker under the Banking Prudential Supervision regime.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Capital injection into the New Zealand operational bank account should be routed via SWIFT MT103 wire transfer (or a cash-letter equivalent) from the Cook Islands/offshore corporate settlor or its trustee, using the ISO 20022 purpose code 'GIFTS' is not appropriate; instead use the true economic purpose under BPM6/New Zealand banking conventions. Acceptable purpose codes or remittance narratives include 'CFER' (capital transfer to related enterprise), 'FDI' (direct investment in operating entity), or 'LOAN/RLOAN' (intercompany loan) depending on whether injection represents equity or debt. The bank must receive a completed source-of-funds declaration, the underlying trust/corporate resolution authorising the capital injection, and an executed treasury instruction with a precise NZD or USD value date. For an International Company relying on tax-exempt-zone classification, the inbound transfer should not be described as a remittance for fine goods/services; it should be tagged to the entity's capital/financing ledger to avoid anti-money-laundering mischaracterisation.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Outbound trade settlement for factoring advances and reverse-factoring payments to suppliers must be executed via SWIFT MT103 single-payment wires for supplier-side disbursements, or by Commercial Letter of Credit (sight or usance) where the factoring transaction is integrated with a trade finance instrument. For NZD payments within New Zealand the domestic clearing rail is the Exchange Settlement Account System (ESAS) operated by the RBNZ, accessed via the corporate bank; for cross-border disbursements denominated in USD, EUR, GBP, or AUD, the payment rail should be a correspondent bank wire (MT103) through the Tier 1 bank's clearing network. To satisfy the 'permissible FX transactions' requirement, each outbound disbursement must have a documented underlying trade receivable or payable, be subject to bank sanctions/dual-use screening, and be accompanied by the transaction invoice, shipping evidence, and reconciliation to the factored receivable ledger.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: FX Forwards (plain vanilla) with a registered New Zealand bank or licensed derivative dealer under the Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013
Cross-currency swaps (CCS / XCCY swaps) for USD-NZD or multi-currency funding mismatches

Non-Deliverable Forwards (NDFs) are not necessary for NZD because the NZD is fully deliverable onshore, but they remain permissible only where counterparty restrictions make deliverable forwards operationally unavailable
FX options (plain vanilla, purchased options) where the underlying commercial exposure arises from cross-border factoring book timing
Centralised treasury netting against natural offsets within the trade receivables portfolio, subject to bank documentation and Master Agreement (ISDA/IFXEMA) execution

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual Return and Annual Government Retention Fee (International Company renewal declaration)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Cook Islands Financial Supervisory Commission - International Companies Registry, through a licensed Cook Islands registered agent
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Anniversary of incorporation; signed return and government fee must be delivered to the registered agent at least five business days before the anniversary date.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late payment triggers an automatic late penalty and, after formal notice by the Registrar, the company may be struck off the International Companies Register if arrears and penalties are not settled within the notice period.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual Tax-Exempt Status Declaration and Non-Resident Business Confirmation
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Cook Islands Financial Supervisory Commission - International Companies Registry, submitted through the registered agent
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Filed concurrently with the Annual Return on the anniversary of incorporation.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: No separate late fee; persistent non-filing may cause the Registrar to treat the company as carrying on domestic business and expose it to Cook Islands income tax, levies, and strike-off proceedings.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual Beneficial Ownership and AML/CFT Re-Confirmation (UBO Register Update)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Cook Islands Financial Supervisory Commission - AML/CFT supervisory records maintained by the licensed registered agent
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Anniversary-based: re-verification must be completed within 28 days after the Annual Return date and immediately upon any share transfer or change in beneficial ownership.
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Failure to maintain accurate UBO records exposes the company and registered agent to AML/CFT fines and remedial orders; continued non-compliance may lead to loss of the registered agent's licence and ultimate strike-off for failure to maintain a registered agent.

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: No statutory audit threshold applies to a standard Cook Islands International Company engaged exclusively in offshore trade-supply-chain factoring. Independent audit is compulsory only if the company is licensed as a bank, insurer, captive insurer, trustee company, or other regulated financial institution; if its constitution or a special resolution requires an audit; or if the Financial Supervisory Commission orders audited financial statements.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: IFRS as issued by the IASB, with New Zealand-equivalent IFRS acceptable in the Cook Islands context; local accounting records must be sufficient to prepare true and fair financial statements, but a standard non-resident International Company is not required to file financial statements publicly.

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: The licensed registered agent must maintain current beneficial ownership information, re-verify each controller at least annually, and update the FSC records before the annual renewal date. Any share transfer requires an executed transfer instrument, approval in accordance with the constitution if required, entry in the Register of Members, and corresponding amendment to the UBO register; the annual confirmation declares that the recorded members and beneficial owners are current.

recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.registered_office_or_agent_market_range_: US$950 - US$1,700 per annum for a licensed Cook Islands registered agent and registered office, excluding government fees
recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.statutory_audit_estimated_fee_usd: Not required for a standard International Company; if audit is triggered by constitution or FSC licence conditions, approximately US$4,500 - US$10,000 for a single-purpose factoring entity

corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: The New Zealand corporate tax system generally provides no broad-based statutory tax holidays or preferential income tax rates for commercial factoring companies. The 28% headline rate applies to all resident companies. Certain tax incentives exist for specific R&D activities under the R&D Tax Incentive regime (a 15% tax credit, refundable in limited circumstances), and the look-through company (LTC) regime enables qualifying closely held companies to attribute income to owners at their individual marginal rates. However, a New Zealand incorporated International Company (IC) engaged in trade supply chain factoring that is centrally managed and controlled in New Zealand will prima facie be tax resident and taxed on worldwide income. A company that is tax resident in New Zealand but exempted from New Zealand tax under a specific statutory exemption or Double Tax Agreement (DTA) category (such as certain offshore-insurance or offshore-trust vehicle arrangements) may claim relief only to the extent expressly authorized by the Inland Revenue Acts and applicable DTA. For factoring income, any interest, discount income, and fees will be taxable at 28% unless a specific exemption applies under sections CW and EX of the Income Tax Act 2007.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: Non-resident and resident companies file IR4 (Company Income Tax Return) via the Inland Revenue Department's (IRD) electronic portal myIR. Certain conduit and portfolio investment entities may file IR4J or supplementary schedules where applicable; a trade factoring International Company will ordinarily use IR4 plus financial statement schedules.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: Generally, the terminal tax and return filing date is 7 months after the company's balance date (e.g., 7 July for a 31 March balance date) for non-provisional taxpayers with a tax agent. For companies with a standard 31 March balance date, the filing deadline is 7 July following the end of the income year. If the company has a tax agent, extension dates may apply under the Tax Administration Act 1994, but the due date for payment of terminal tax remains aligned to the 7-month rule unless a provisional tax payment schedule applies. For companies required to pay provisional tax (non-resident withholding income or high residual income tax), the instalment rules under the Tax Administration Act 1994 and Income Tax Act 2007 apply.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Enter the legal name exactly as registered on the New Zealand Companies Register and the IRD number. A non-resident company with a New Zealand permanent establishment (PE) must register for IRD purposes and quote its non-resident company code.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Income tax return type indicator (IR4 or IR4J)
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Select IR4; non-resident companies must also complete the Non-Resident Company Return (IR4N or supplementary page) if they have a PE in New Zealand and are not fully resident.
State the 12-month accounting period. A non-resident IC with an off-cycle balance date should follow the IRD-approved substituted accounting period.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Total income (gross income from business, interest, dividends, royalties, factoring fees and discount income)
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Declare all New Zealand-source gross income, including factoring discount charges, administration fees, interest and arrangement commissions. Foreign-source income attributable to a New Zealand PE must be included if the non-resident is deemed resident for treaty purposes or effectively connected to the PE.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Total expenses (deductions including financing costs, bad debts, administrative overheads, and any deductible impairment allowance under financial arrangement rules)
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Only deduct expenses incurred in deriving assessable income and satisfying the general permission under section DA 1 Income Tax Act 2007. Cross-border management fees are deductible subject to transfer pricing and dividend withholding payment (DWP) rules and the non-resident's Schedule 8 or tax agent review.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Net taxable income (assessable income minus allowable deductions)
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Computed after applying the financial arrangement rules (FA rules) under sections EW 1–EW 58, which require spreading of discount/premium income on receivables over the life of the arrangement using a yield-to-maturity basis unless a permitted straight-line or cash basis election is made.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Loss offset / net losses carried forward
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Loss offsets are available under the group loss offset rules (subpart IC) or continuity of ownership rules (section IA 5). Non-resident companies carrying forward losses must satisfy the 49% shareholder continuity test. Only 5 years of loss carryforward is assumed per the schema, although New Zealand statutory rules do not impose a 5-year expiry for most losses.
Enter the final figure subject to 28% corporate tax. If a DTA article limits New Zealand's taxing right to business profits attributable to a PE, compute only the attributable profit.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Foreign income tax credits, imputation credits and RWT credits
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-residents may claim foreign tax credits under section LJ for foreign income taxed in the source state. Imputation credits attached to New Zealand dividends are non-refundable to non-resident shareholders and only offset corporate tax if the company is itself a shareholder. Provide underlying schedules.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Tax payable / terminal tax or refund due
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Calculate residual income tax after credits. Non-resident companies must settle terminal tax by due date; payments of resident withholding tax (RWT) on interest or dividends and non-resident withholding tax (NRWT) may be required at earlier points.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late filing penalty under the Tax Administration Act 1994 for non-electronic returns is NZ$250 for the first day and NZ$50 per day up to NZ$2,500 for each month (or part-month) the return remains unfiled; for large taxpayers (gross income over NZ$5 million) the penalty is increased. In addition, late payment of tax triggers an initial late payment penalty: 1% of the unpaid tax on the due day, then 4% after 7 days, followed by an incremental 1% per month until paid. An assessment made by the Commissioner can be increased by 20% if the tax shortfall arises from an unacceptable tax position without reasonable care, and up to 150% for evasion or an abusive tax position. Use of a tax agent does not remove the company's liability for penalties.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: Non-resident withholding tax (NRWT) applies to dividends paid by a New Zealand resident company to a non-resident shareholder. The statutory rate is 15% for fully imputed dividends where the company has attached imputation credits on an imputation account balance sufficient to fully impute the dividend, and 30% on non-imputed dividends and for dividends declared from retained earnings with no imputation credit. The standard NRWT rate under the Income Tax Act 2007 and the NRWT rules is 15% for fully imputed dividends paid to a resident of a treaty country or under an approved issuer levy (AIL) regime, but 30% is the default for unfranked/non-imputed dividends unless a lower treaty rate applies. Under the New Zealand–Hong Kong DTA (which would govern a CK_IC International Company with a Hong Kong/offshore parent), the dividend withholding tax rate may be reduced to 0% or 5% depending on the level of shareholding, but note the DTA does not apply unless the recipient is the beneficial owner and is a resident of the other contracting state. For a domestic New Zealand entity structured as an International Company with ultimate non-resident ownership, dividend repatriation to the foreign parent falls under NRWT, unless the portfolio investment entity or supplementary dividend regime applies (not available for straight factoring).
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: To invoke DTA relief, the non-resident recipient must complete an IRD Form IR472 (Certificate of Residence / Tax Residency Certificate from the jurisdiction of residence) and provide it to the New Zealand payer before the dividend, interest, or royalty payment is made. The payer must withhold NRWT at the domestic statutory rate unless it has received a valid notice from the Commissioner or is satisfied the recipient is entitled to treaty benefits. For lower treaty rates, the payer must hold a completed IR472 and may also need a declaration of beneficial ownership. Where a claim is made after the payment, the non-resident may seek a refund from the IRD for the excess NRWT within the statutory time bar (generally 4 years from the end of the tax year in which the payment was made). Certain treaty benefits are subject to limitation-of-benefits (LOB) or principal purpose clauses (PPT) in New Zealand's DTAs; a Hong Kong parent company must have substantive economic activity to obtain treaty relief. The Inland Revenue may issue a determination or require a binding ruling under sections 90AA–91G of the Tax Administration Act 1994 for unusual cross-border structures.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Statutory NRWT on interest is 15% under the Income Tax Act 2007 when paid to a non-resident (and an Approved Issuer Levy (AIL) of 2% can be paid instead by New Zealand resident issuers on offshore borrowing, effectively eliminating NRWT on interest). Cross-border royalties are subject to NRWT at 15% (and are also assessable under the royalty withholding rules in section RF 2C). Approved Issuer Levy does not apply to royalties. Under the New Zealand–Hong Kong DTA, interest may be taxed at a maximum rate of 10% (or 0% in certain cases on government or approved entities), and royalties at 5% (or 0% for certain copyright/trade royalties). A non-resident factoring company receiving factoring discount income may not categorise the entire margin as 'interest' for treaty purposes; because factoring discount is consideration for the purchase of receivables, it is generally treated as business profits under Article 7 of the DTA and is taxable in New Zealand only if attributable to a permanent establishment. If the factoring arrangement is legally structured as a loan (debt finance), the discount/margin constitutes interest and is subject to NRWT at the domestic 15% rate, with a 10% DTA ceiling. The correct characterisation is determined by economic substance and the financial arrangement rules.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: New Zealand has no mandatory statutory thresholds that expressly require Local File or Master File on the OECD-aligned basis for all taxpayers; transfer pricing documentation must be prepared and retained by taxpayers who have international related party dealings, applying the OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines. However, the Inland Revenue's Administrative Guidelines (and the OECD's Country-by-Country (CbC) Reporting rules adopted in New Zealand) trigger mandatory CbC documentation for multinational groups with consolidated group revenue of NZ$1.125 billion or more (including non-resident groups operating in New Zealand). For local file/master file purposes, the Commissioner can request documentation under section 9 of the Tax Administration Act 1994, and the taxpayer must provide it within a reasonable time. The practical safe harbor threshold used by the IRD to reduce TP compliance burdens is NZ$3 million in aggregate non-risk-related cross-border related party transactions (or $15 million for low-risk routine financing transactions) for a simplified contemporaneous documentation requirement, but this is administrative guidance rather than a statutory threshold. For a trade supply chain factoring IC, if it enters into cross-border factoring transactions with related parties (e.g., purchases or discounts receivables from a foreign affiliate), it must comply with Part 4A of the Income Tax Act 2007 (transfer pricing rules) regardless of size.
approved_arm_length_methodologies: CUP, Resale Price, Cost Plus, TNMM, Profit Split
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: New Zealand does not have a separate 'Economic Substance Regulations' (ESR) statute equivalent to the UAE or Crown Dependencies; instead, the Inland Revenue applies the general anti-avoidance rule (GAAR) under section BG 1 and sections GA 1, GB 1 of the Income Tax Act 2007, plus the transfer pricing rules, the non-resident company attribution rules, and the DTA limitation-of-benefits provisions. A factoring International Company must demonstrate real economic substance in New Zealand: substantive decision-making, employees, premises, and operational functions must be present if it claims New Zealand residence benefits (e.g., treaty access). If the entity has no commercial substance and is used solely to avoid tax or obtain tax benefits, the Commissioner may reconstruct the arrangement under the GAAR or apply the OECD/G20 BEPS multilateral instrument (MLI) principal purpose test. For New Zealand purposes, the 'economic substance doctrine' is effectively codified in the business continuity and residency tests, and the IRD may disregard a shell entity under the general anti-avoidance provisions. The Companies Act 1993 also allows the court to pierce the corporate veil for sham or facade arrangements.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Structuring the factoring IC as a shell company in New Zealand to book profits from cross-border receivables while management and control (and all economic substance) remain offshore, or using artificial intercompany pricing to shift profits out of New Zealand without arm's length remuneration.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Under section 141 of the Tax Administration Act 1994, evasion or similar offence carries a penalty of up to 100% of the resulting tax shortfall (or 150% for abusive tax positions under section 141D). Criminal prosecution under section 143A can impose a maximum fine of NZ$50,000 for individuals and NZ$250,000 for companies, and imprisonment for up to 5 years for individuals. The Commissioner may also issue a default assessment to the maximum amount, cancel tax losses, and deny deductions. For failure to keep adequate tax records, a penalty of up to NZ$20,000 may apply under section 139AA, and daily penalties of NZ$500 can be imposed for failure to supply information under Section 19 or 21.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors may be personally liable under the Companies Act 1993 for allowing the company to trade recklessly or incur obligations without reasonable grounds (section 135), and for the company's tax debts if they signed a declaration of solvency or caused the company to avoid tax. The Tax Administration Act 1994 (section 163A) provides that directors and officers can be jointly and severally liable for certain PAYE, GST, RWT, and NRWT amounts withheld from others but not remitted. Under section 143A, directors of a company convicted of tax evasion may be imprisoned for up to 5 years. Civil penalties can include repayment of tax shortfalls plus interest under section 12 of the Interest on Tax (IOT) provisions (currently 7% per annum initially, adjustable quarterly). The Commissioner may also obtain a civil judgment and bankruptcy or liquidation orders; directors may face travel bans under the Summary Proceedings Act 1957 only after court-ordered examination or where they have failed to comply with an IRD investigation summons, and exit orders are available under the Tax Administration Act 1994 for deliberate tax defaulters with outstanding debt exceeding NZ$10,000.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Applying unrealistic margins on cross-border factoring receivables, failing to prepare contemporaneous transfer pricing documentation, or failing to align profits with the economically significant risks assumed by the New Zealand entity (e.g., sole relationship to a Hong Kong parent without bearing credit risk or having capital).
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Under sections GC 6–GC 14 and Part 4A of the Income Tax Act 2007, the Commissioner may adjust the taxpayer's transfer price to the arm's length amount, increasing taxable income and imposing shortfall penalties. The shortfall penalty for not taking reasonable care is 20% (section 141B); for unacceptable tax positions, 20%; for abusive tax positions, 50%; and for evasion or fraudulent intent, 100% (section 141E). The IRD may also impose late payment penalties and use-of-money interest on the increased tax assessment. Failure to provide documentation may result in an adverse inference and higher penalties because the taxpayer cannot demonstrate reasonableness.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who knowingly participate in preparing false transfer pricing documentation or causing the company to file an inaccurate tax return may be personally liable for penalties as an aider and abettor under sections 141 and 144 of the Tax Administration Act 1994. If the company is liquidated, directors can be personally liable for tax debts under section 165 of the Companies Act 1993 (reckless trading) or section 300 for debts incurred while insolvent. Overseas travel bans can be imposed by the High Court for failure to comply with discovery orders, and directors may be disqualified from managing companies for up to 5 years under section 383 of the Companies Act 1993.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: AML/CFT and Regulatory Breach (Factoring as Money Remittance / Lending)
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Operating an accounts receivable factoring and reverse factoring business without the required registration under the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009 (AML/CFT Act) or the Financial Service Providers (Registration and Dispute Resolution) Act 2008 (FSP Act), failing to conduct customer due diligence, or processing payments through escrow/SWIFT rails without an anti-money laundering programme.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Under the AML/CFT Act 2009, a financial institution (including a factoring entity that provides financial services by lending or providing financial accommodation) that fails to register or comply with its AML/CFT obligations may be subject to civil liability of up to NZ$2 million for a body corporate per contravention (section 89), and directors/officers can be fined up to NZ$300,000 (section 90). Failure to report suspicious transactions is a criminal offence with a maximum penalty of 2 years' imprisonment and a fine of NZ$10,000 (section 90A), and breaches of the identity verification and record-keeping requirements attract civil penalties up to NZ$100,000. The Financial Markets Authority (FMA) and Department of Internal Affairs supervise enforcement, and a contravention may also constitute a criminal offence under the Financial Transactions Reporting Act. The FSP Act requires registration on the Financial Service Providers Register (FSPR) for providing factoring services; unregistered provision of financial services can lead to a compliance order from the FMA or a fine of up to NZ$500,000. The Commerce Commission can also levy penalties for misleading conduct in trade finance promotional statements under the Fair Trading Act 1986: up to NZ$200,000 for individuals and NZ$600,000 for companies per breach.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors can be personally liable for AML/CFT civil penalties under section 90 AML/CFT Act if they knew or ought reasonably to have known that the company was breaching its obligations, and criminal liability with imprisonment up to 2 years applies for knowingly providing misleading information. Under the FSP Act, directors who provide unregistered financial services commit an offence and may be personally fined up to NZ$300,000. If the company is used as a shell to move funds without appropriate AML controls, directors may additionally be charged with money laundering offences under the Crimes Act 1961 (sections 243–245), which carry a maximum penalty of 7 years' imprisonment; the criminal proceeds can be restrained or forfeited under the Criminal Proceeds (Recovery) Act 2009. Travel bans may be imposed under the Bail Act and criminal justice procedures; the High Court may order surrender of passports in relation to extradition or proceeds-of-crime investigations.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Shell Company / Lack of Economic Substance (Corporate Veil Piercing)
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Using the New Zealand IC as a mere nominee, agent, or bare trustee for a non-resident parent with no employees, premises, or substantive operations; entering into factoring arrangements that are entirely administered offshore while claiming New Zealand residency and treaty benefits; or capitalizing the IC with zero capital despite exercising large credit and default risks.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The Companies Act 1993 allows the court to pierce the corporate veil in cases of fraud, sham, or where the company is an alter ego. The Inland Revenue may reconstruct the arrangement under the general anti-avoidance provision (section BG 1) and section GB 1, treating the income as derived by the controlling persons. The New Zealand tax law also contains the 'branch equivalent' and 'controlled foreign company' (CFC) attribution rules (sections EX 1–EX 24B) that can attribute the passive or factoring income of a controlled non-resident company to New Zealand residents. The penalty for a company being a facade is the cancellation of tax benefits and assessment of tax as if the arrangement had not occurred; the Commissioner can issue assessments on a reconstruction basis, even on a gross basis. A finding of sham exposes the IC to an interlocutory declaration that the entity has no legal existence for tax purposes, and all income becomes taxable in the hands of the beneficial owner, with potential penalties up to 150% under the abusive tax position rules.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors of a sham/shell IC face personal liability at common law for misrepresentation, and under sections 135, 137, and 301 of the Companies Act 1993 can be held liable to repay company debts or compensate the company for losses caused by reckless or fraudulent conduct. Under the Tax Administration Act 1994, directors can be held personally liable in respect of unpaid tax where the company's tax avoidance arrangement is deemed a sham and the director was knowingly party to it. Civil penalties cannot be discharged by corporate liquidation. Travel restrictions apply: the High Court may, on application of the IRD or the Serious Fraud Office, make a travel ban order under section 55 of the Tax Administration Act 1994 against a director who is a New Zealand tax defaulter, or under the Mutual Assistance in Criminal Matters Act 1992 if extradition proceedings arise from tax evasion charges (maximum imprisonment for tax evasion is 5 years; for serious fraud under the Crimes Act it is 7 years). Directors may also be disqualified from acting as directors for up to 10 years under the Companies Act 1993 in connection with their management of a company that is deregistered for tax offences.
